## Learning Objectives

- Compare and contrast the terms "parameter" and "statistic".
- Determine whether a quantity is a parameter or statistic.


## Lesson

A parameter is a function of a population.
For example, the expected value is a parameter.
A statistic is a function of a sample.
For example, the sample average is a statistic.

Unfortunately, it is often the case that the same word could be a parameter
or statistic depending on context.
Consider the median.
Every population distribution has a median.
For a continuous random variable,
the area under the curve to the right of the median is 0.5.
(The definition of the median for a discrete random variable
is more complicated,
so I'm just going to avoid it for now.)

Every sample has a median, too.
To get the sample median, you line up all the values in the sample
from smallest to largest.
If there are $n$ observations, and $n$ is odd,
the median is the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value in the list.
For example, in the data set $\{0,3,4,5,15\}$,
the median is 4.
If there are $n$ observations, and $n$ is even,
the median is the average of the $\frac{n}{2}$th
and $\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)$th values in the list.
For example, in the data set $\{0,3,4,5,15,24\}$,
the median is
$$
\frac{4 + 5}{2} = 4.5 \text{.}
$$




## Problems

### Problem 1

Is the maximum value in my sample a parameter or a statistic?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

It's a statistic, because it's something you computed from your data.

:::

### Problem 2

In clinical trials, we often want to know the expected difference
in some outcome (e.g., blood pressure, risk of death)
between people who take a drug and people who don't
Is this a parameter or a statistic?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

This is a parameter.
If we randomly assign some people to receive a drug and some people to
receive a placebo,
and then compute the difference between the averages of the outcome
across the groups,
that would be a statistic.

:::
